ghost.currentMeaning: An apparition of a dead person; a spirit

chain.note: The root: the feeling of terror and wonder
The spirit as breath — the exhalation of dying, the last gasp. A ghost was originally the breath that left the body at death.
Also meant 'breath' — the word captured the exhalation of dying, the moment soul left body
The meaning narrowed toward 'spectral apparition'

chain.meaning: an apparition of a dead person
chain.note: A ghost is a breath that refused to leave. The word originally meant the breath of life — the spirit that animates. Now it means the spirit that haunts. William Tyndale used 'Holy Ghost' in his Bible translation, preserving the older 'spirit' meaning alongside the haunted one.

deadBranches.note: A verb form that didn't survive into Modern English
The original non-scary meaning — breath, the life force — is dead. 'Ghost' now only means something frightening. The Holy Ghost preserves the older, neutral sense.

salary.currentMeaning: A fixed regular payment earned for work

chain.note: Salt was currency before currency existed. It preserved food, sustained armies, and built trade routes.
The root visible in 'salary', 'saline', 'salami', 'salt'
Roman soldiers received a 'salarium' — originally an allowance for salt, later any regular payment. Whether it was literally salt rations or money in lieu of salt is debated, but the name stuck.
The salt was forgotten; only the money remained

chain.meaning: a fixed regular payment for work
chain.note: Every payday, you are literally collecting salt money from a 2000-year-old Roman military logistics system. The word 'salt' is visible in 'salary' — 'sal' is right there.

deadBranches.note: A related Latin word for salt-works — the industrial infrastructure of salt production — died without entering modern languages. Only the military payment survived.

disaster.currentMeaning: A sudden event causing great damage or suffering

chain.note: Ancient peoples believed stars controlled human fate. A bad star meant a bad life.
The Greek word for star, giving us 'astronomy', 'astronaut', 'asterisk'
The root that gives us astronomy, astrology, astronaut
'Dis-' (against, bad) + 'astro' (star). When the stars were against you, that was a disaster.
Borrowed from Italian with the astrological meaning intact

chain.meaning: a sudden event causing great damage
chain.note: Every disaster is a bad star. The star in 'disaster' is the same star in 'astronomy'. Ancient astrology is still inside every modern catastrophe.

deadBranches.note: The original literal sense — a specific bad astrological conjunction — is dead. The word has generalized from 'bad star' to 'any catastrophe'. The astrology is fossil.

companion.currentMeaning: A person with whom one spends time or travels

chain.note: Feeding as the fundamental act of care
The root that also gives us 'pantry', 'panini', 'paneer'
'Com-' (with) + 'panis' (bread). A companion is literally someone you break bread with. The deepest social bond reduced to its simplest act.
The word traveled with feudal military culture — companions in arms shared rations

chain.meaning: a person with whom one spends time
chain.note: Your companions are still, etymologically, your bread-sharers. The Latin 'panis' (bread) is still visible inside 'companion'. Every meal with a friend reenacts the word's origin.

deadBranches.meaning: body of soldiers, band of companions
deadBranches.note: This became 'company' — the corporate sense (a business company) is a dead metaphor from military fellowship

muscle.currentMeaning: A body tissue that contracts to produce movement

chain.note: The mouse — small, rounded, scurrying under surfaces
Greek physicians noticed the resemblance: a flexing muscle under the skin moves like a mouse. Same word, two meanings.
Roman anatomists translated the Greek metaphor literally: 'mus' (mouse) + '-culus' (diminutive). A muscle is a 'little mouse' running under your skin.
Borrowed directly from Latin medical terminology
Every time you flex, a little mouse is running under your skin. That's what the Romans saw, and they named it accordingly. The metaphor has survived 2000 years.

deadBranches.note: The same 'little mouse' metaphor was also applied to shellfish that clamped shut. This sense survives in 'mussel' via a different path.

clue.currentMeaning: A piece of evidence that helps solve a problem or mystery

chain.meaning: a ball of thread or yarn
chain.note: A simple word for a simple object. The detective meaning was centuries away.
Still just yarn. No metaphor yet.

chain.meaning: a ball of thread; a guide through a maze
chain.note: The myth of Theseus and the Minotaur — where Ariadne gives Theseus a ball of thread to navigate the labyrinth — gave 'clew' its metaphorical meaning: something that guides you through a maze of questions.

chain.meaning: a piece of evidence used in solving a problem
chain.note: The spelling shifted from 'clew' to 'clue'. The thread was forgotten. A clue is a fossil of Ariadne's ball of yarn, compressed into four letters.

deadBranches.note: The literal meaning — a ball of yarn — is now completely dead in English. The metaphor consumed the original word.

daisy.currentMeaning: A small grassland flower with yellow center and white petals

chain.note: The flower opens in the morning and closes at night. Anglo-Saxons named it for this: the eye of the day, watching the sun.
Compounded into a single word — the day's eye became one thing
The compound fused phonetically. Speakers forgot it meant 'day's eye'.
A daisy is a day's eye that forgot it was watching. One of the most literal flower names in English, now invisible.

deadBranches.meaning: the sun itself (the day's eye in the sky)
deadBranches.note: The phrase could also mean the sun itself — the day's eye in the sky. That poetic sense died with Old English.

chain.note: 'Ne-' (not) + 'scire' (to know). The original meaning: not knowing. Ignorant.
The word drifted: from 'ignorant' to 'foolish' to 'simple'. Not a compliment.
Borrowed from French. Then the drift began: foolish → timid → fastidious → precise.
A 'nice distinction' meant a precise one. Jane Austen used 'nice' this way.

The greatest semantic drift in English. From 'ignorant' to 'pleasant' in 1800 years. Jane Austen complained about people who used 'nice' to mean 'pleasant' — she preferred the older 'precise' meaning.

cognates.meaning: I don't know (preserved original Latin sense)

deadBranches.note: In the 14th century, 'nice' could mean sexually promiscuous — the opposite of today's meaning. This sense vanished without a trace.

quarantine.currentMeaning: A period of isolation to prevent the spread of disease

chain.note: The number four underlies the word — specifically, forty days
Forty days had biblical resonance: Jesus in the desert, the flood, Moses on Sinai
Ships arriving in Venice during the plague were required to anchor offshore for 40 days before landing
The Venetian quarantine law of 1448 formalized the practice. The word became inseparable from disease prevention.

chain.meaning: period of isolation to prevent disease spread
chain.note: The forty days became symbolic — modern quarantines can be any length, but the number four is still locked inside the word.

deadBranches.meaning: a period of forty days (any forty-day period, not just medical)
deadBranches.note: In older French, 'quarantaine' could mean any forty-day stretch — a fasting period, a legal term, a Lenten observance. The medical sense won.

sycophant.currentMeaning: A person who flatters someone important to gain advantage

chain.note: A fig. The word starts here, with a fruit.
'Sykon' (fig) + 'phainein' (to show). In Athens, someone who informed on illegal fig exporters — or possibly someone who pointed out stolen figs. A petty snitch.

chain.meaning: a base accuser, a malicious informer
chain.note: Generalized: any professional informant or false accuser. The fig was forgotten; the sneaking remained.
Borrowed from Greek as a legal term
The meaning shifted from 'informer' toward 'flatterer' — someone who whispers to power
From fig-informer to yes-man. The journey: fig → fig-snitch → snitch → flatterer. Every sycophant carries a forgotten fig.

deadBranches.meaning: to inform against someone, to accuse falsely
deadBranches.note: The Greek verb form — the act of fig-informing — is dead even in Greek

chain.note: The number three, fundamental and ordinary

chain.meaning: crossroads, place where three roads meet
chain.note: 'Tri-' (three) + 'via' (road). A crossroads was a public, ordinary place where anyone could gather.
Something 'trivial' belonged to the crossroads — common, public, unspecialized. The word for 'ordinary' became the word for 'unimportant'.

chain.meaning: the three liberal arts: grammar, logic, rhetoric
chain.note: In medieval universities, the trivium was the introductory three subjects — basic, foundational, 'trivial'
Three roads meet. The meeting place is ordinary. The ordinary is unimportant. That's how 'three roads' became 'meaningless'.

deadBranches.meaning: Diana as goddess of the crossroads
deadBranches.note: The Roman goddess Trivia (Diana/Artemis at three-way crossroads) — a divine epithet that became the English word 'trivia' (unimportant facts), completing the degradation from goddess to pub quiz

chain.note: Pastoral life: herds, grazing, the shepherd's world

chain.meaning: the god of shepherds, flocks, and wild places
chain.note: Pan — half-goat, half-man — was the god of the wilderness. His appearance caused terror.
Sudden, irrational fear was attributed to Pan — the god who startled shepherds and spread fear through armies
Borrowed from Greek via Latin, carrying the divine origin with it
Every panic attack is, etymologically, a visit from Pan. The goat-god is still startling us.

deadBranches.meaning: terror sent by Pan (specifically in military contexts)
deadBranches.note: Ancient armies attributed sudden, irrational retreats to Pan — a divine panic that spread through ranks without cause

candidate.currentMeaning: A person who applies for a job or is nominated for election

chain.note: The root that gives us 'candle', 'incandescent', and 'candid' — all about white light
White as purity. White as visibility. White as virtue.
Roman political candidates wore specially whitened togas to signal their purity and suitability for office. Campaigning in a white toga — the original white candidacy.
The white toga was gone, but the word for 'man in white' became the word for 'office-seeker'

chain.meaning: a person who seeks or is nominated for a position
chain.note: Every candidate is, etymologically, a person dressed in white. The Roman campaign strategy of wearing a bright toga is frozen in the word forever.

deadBranches.meaning: a person dressed in white (general sense)
deadBranches.note: The original meaning — simply someone wearing white clothes — is completely lost. Only the political sense survives.

gossip.currentMeaning: Casual or unconstrained conversation about other people

chain.note: 'God' + 'sibb' (related, kin). A godsibb was your spiritual relative — the person who stood with you at a christening.
The religious meaning softened. A gossip was a close friend — the person you talked to, trusted, confided in.
By Shakespeare's time, the word had flipped. The person you confided in became the person who talked too much. Trust became tattling.

chain.meaning: casual talk about other people's lives
chain.note: From god's kin to idle talk. The journey: godparent → close friend → confidante → chatterbox → rumour. The sacred became the scandalous.

deadBranches.meaning: a woman attending childbirth to offer support
deadBranches.note: In medieval England, a 'gossip' was specifically a woman who attended a friend in childbirth — a spiritual companion for the ordeal. This meaning died completely.

robot.currentMeaning: A machine capable of carrying out complex actions automatically

chain.note: Feudal peasants owed 'robota' — compulsory labor — to their lords. The word tasted like exhaustion.
Still in use, still meaning hard, obligatory work
Karel Čapek coined 'robot' in his play R.U.R. (Rossum's Universal Robots) from 'robota'. His machines were created to do forced labor — the word was chosen to mean 'slave worker'.
Čapek's robots weren't mechanical — they were biological, made of synthetic flesh. The machine sense came later. A 20th-century word with an old soul: forced labor, frozen into metal.

deadBranches.note: The root 'rob' (slave) is archaic in Czech — the feudal system that created it is gone, but 'robota' (labor) survived

sincere.currentMeaning: Free from pretence or deceit; genuine

chain.note: The origin is disputed. One theory: 'sine cera' (without wax) — Roman sculptors filled flaws in marble with wax. Sincere marble was flawless. Another theory: the word is simply old Latin with no clear etymology.
The physical meaning (pure, unmixed) developed a moral meaning (honest, genuine).
Borrowed from Latin with the moral meaning dominant

Whether or not the 'sine cera' (without wax) story is true, it's been told for 2000 years. The word means 'without wax' in the popular imagination — and that story has become part of the word's meaning.

deadBranches.note: The original physical sense — pure honey, unmixed wine, unblemished marble — died as the word moved into moral territory

assassin.currentMeaning: A person who murders a public figure for political or religious motives

chain.note: A sect of Ismaili Shia Muslims, the Nizari, were called 'hashish eaters' by their enemies. Whether they actually used hashish is disputed — it may have been propaganda.
Crusaders brought stories of the 'Assassins' back to Europe — a fearsome sect whose agents would publicly kill their enemies
The word generalized from the specific sect to any murderer who kills for a cause

chain.meaning: a person who murders for political or religious motives
chain.note: The hashish is long gone. But the word still carries the traces of a Crusader-era smear campaign against a Persian mountain sect.

deadBranches.meaning: specifically a member of the Nizari Ismaili order
deadBranches.note: The original meaning — a specific religious sect based in Alamut, Persia — is dead. The word became so generic that its origin is forgotten.

algorithm.currentMeaning: A process or set of rules to be followed in calculations

chain.meaning: Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwārizmī, Persian mathematician
chain.note: Al-Khwārizmī wrote a book on Hindu-Arabic numerals that introduced algebra to the Islamic world and, through translation, to Europe. His name became a word.

chain.meaning: the system of Arabic numerals and calculation
chain.note: Latin translators of al-Khwārizmī's work Latinized his name. 'Algorismus' meant doing arithmetic with Arabic numerals (as opposed to the abacus).
The word traveled through France, still meaning the specific practice of doing math with numerals rather than counting boards
The spelling shifted (influenced by Greek 'arithmos' — number) and the meaning generalized from Arabic numerals to any systematic procedure

chain.meaning: a process or set of rules for calculation or problem-solving
chain.note: A 9th-century Persian mathematician's name became the word that defines the digital age. Al-Khwārizmī is still computing.

deadBranches.meaning: the specific practice of calculation with Hindu-Arabic numerals
deadBranches.note: The original meaning — a specific system of writing and manipulating numbers — died as the word abstracted. We forgot it was once about the number system itself, not just procedures.

avocado.currentMeaning: A pear-shaped tropical fruit with green flesh

chain.note: The Aztecs named the avocado for its resemblance to a testicle. The word meant both the fruit and the anatomy.
Spanish colonists borrowed the Nahuatl word and modified its pronunciation. The anatomical meaning was politely forgotten.
The spelling shifted, possibly influenced by Spanish 'abogado' (lawyer) — a folk reshaping that disguised the origin further
Every avocado toast carries a hidden Nahuatl anatomical joke.

deadBranches.note: The original anatomical meaning is completely lost in English, though Nahuatl speakers would have found avocado marketing campaigns very funny

orange.currentMeaning: A round citrus fruit with tough bright reddish-yellow skin

chain.note: The word traveled with the fruit along trade routes from India to the Mediterranean
Persian traders carried both the fruit and its name westward
Arabic added the definite article: 'al-nāranj'. The fruit reached Europe through Islamic Sicily and Spain.
The Arabic 'n' dropped under French phonological pressure. The color was named after the fruit, not the other way around.
Before oranges reached England, there was no English word for the color orange. Things were 'yellow-red'. The fruit gave us the color. A Sanskrit word for a tree became the name of a color.

deadBranches.note: French originally called the fruit 'pomme d'orenge' (orange apple) before shortening. The 'apple' part was dropped — it didn't survive the journey.

whiskey.currentMeaning: A spirit distilled from malted grain

chain.note: The Celtic word for water — the basis of life
In medieval Irish monasteries, monks distilled a spirit they called 'uisce beatha' — water of life
A calque on Latin 'aqua vitae'. The Irish monks who invented whiskey called it the water of life.
The phrase spread to Scotland. 'Uisge' was pronounced roughly 'ish-kyə'.
English borrowed the phrase whole: 'usquebaugh' was the anglicized form of 'uisge beatha'
'Usquebaugh' shortened to 'whiskey'. The 'water of life' is still inside the word, compressed into six letters. Every glass of whiskey is a glass of life-water.

deadBranches.meaning: medicinal distillation (used by monks as medicine)
deadBranches.note: The original monastic context — whiskey as a medicinal elixir distilled by monks — is entirely gone from the modern drinking culture

sarcasm.currentMeaning: The use of irony to mock or convey contempt

chain.note: The root: literally cutting meat, tearing flesh from bone

chain.meaning: to tear flesh, to gnash the teeth
chain.note: Literally: to rend meat from bone. The word for butchery became the word for verbal cruelty.
The metaphorical leap: cutting with words instead of teeth. A sarcastic remark is a verbal wound.
Borrowed from Greek as a rhetorical term

chain.meaning: the use of irony to mock or convey contempt
chain.note: The flesh-tearing is still inside the word. A sarcastic comment is, etymologically, a bite. The teeth are hidden in the grammar.

deadBranches.note: The original physical meaning — literally ripping meat — is completely dead. The word exists only as metaphor now.

lunatic.currentMeaning: Mentally ill; extremely foolish (archaic and offensive)

chain.note: The root that gives us 'light', 'lucid', and 'lunar'
The Romans believed moonlight caused madness. Lunacy was literally moon-sickness.
A lunatic was someone whose mind was affected by the phases of the moon. The full moon was thought to trigger episodes.
The word traveled with the belief. Medieval medicine still attributed mental illness to lunar influence.
The moon is still in the word. Every time someone says 'lunatic', they're invoking a 2000-year-old theory that moonlight causes madness.

deadBranches.note: Roman physicians classified certain periodic illnesses as 'lunaticus' — tied to lunar cycles. This medical classification died with ancient medicine, but the word survived as an insult.

chain.note: In Homer's Odyssey, Mentor was the trusted friend of Odysseus who guided his son Telemachus. The goddess Athena often disguised herself as Mentor.
The character's name became a common noun. A 'mentor' was any wise guide.
The word entered modern European languages through French literary culture's rediscovery of classical texts
The word's popularity was boosted by François Fénelon's 1699 novel 'Les Aventures de Télémaque', where Mentor plays an expanded role. A 2700-year-old fictional character became a generic noun.

deadBranches.note: The character was a real person in the fiction of the Odyssey — a specific Ithacan nobleman. That specificity is dead. He exists now only as a function: advising.

pencil.currentMeaning: An instrument for writing or drawing with a solid core in a wooden case

chain.note: 'Peniculus' (brush) + diminutive suffix. A penicillus was a small brush used for painting — literally a 'little tail' of hair.
The word narrowed to mean specifically an artist's brush for fine work
English borrowed the French word for an artist's brush. A pencil was for painting, not writing.
When graphite deposits were discovered in England, the writing instrument we now call a pencil was invented. The old 'brush' word was repurposed for the new technology.

chain.meaning: a writing instrument with graphite core
chain.note: A pencil is a little tail. The original Latin 'penicillus' — a brush shaped like a tiny tail of animal hair — gave its name to a graphite stick in wood. The tail is still there.

deadBranches.meaning: a small paintbrush for fine art
deadBranches.note: The original meaning — a fine brush for painting — is dead in English. French 'pinceau' still means 'paintbrush', preserving the older sense that English has lost.

sophisticated.currentMeaning: Having refined worldly knowledge; complex or advanced

chain.note: The root: wisdom, cleverness. But wisdom has always had two faces — true insight and clever deceit.

chain.meaning: sophist, a paid teacher of rhetoric
chain.note: The Sophists were itinerant teachers who sold wisdom. Plato despised them — he said they made the weaker argument appear stronger. 'Sophist' became a smear.

chain.meaning: adulterated, corrupted, mixed with inferior material
chain.note: The Latin past participle meant 'falsified' — sophistry as intellectual fraud. A 'sophisticated' wine was one that had been watered down.
To sophisticate something was to make it worse — to fake it, to dilute it.

The word flipped completely. From 'adulterated fraud' to 'refined elegance' in 2000 years. The journey: wise → clever → deceitful → adulterated → falsified → worldly → refined. The sophists won in the end.

deadBranches.meaning: to adulterate, to debase by mixing with inferior material
deadBranches.note: The original English meaning — to falsify or adulterate — is completely dead. A 'sophisticated' drug used to mean a diluted one. Now it means the opposite of diluted.

jeans.currentMeaning: Hard-wearing casual trousers made of denim

chain.note: Genoa was a major textile center. Sailors and workers wore tough cloth from the city.

chain.meaning: a twilled cotton cloth from Genoa
chain.note: The city name became the fabric name. 'Jean' was the material, not the garment.
The fabric name transferred to the garment. Jeans are named after Genoa, Italy. Every pair of jeans carries the name of an Italian port city.

deadBranches.meaning: a type of fabric (not a garment)
deadBranches.note: The original meaning — the cloth itself, not the pants — is dead. 'Jean' used to be a material like 'cotton' or 'linen'. Now it's only the garment.

malaria.currentMeaning: A serious tropical disease transmitted by mosquitoes

chain.note: Medieval Italians believed the disease was caused by the foul air around swamps and marshes. The 'miasma theory' of disease blamed bad air for everything.

chain.meaning: the disease caused by bad air
chain.note: The phrase fused into one word. The theory was wrong — mosquitoes, not air, spread the disease — but the name stuck.
The bad air theory died. The mosquitoes were identified. But the word still says 'bad air' — a fossil of dead science, preserved in modern medicine.

cognates.meaning: malaria (from Latin palus — swamp, different root)

deadBranches.meaning: any bad air, any unhealthy atmosphere
deadBranches.note: The original meaning — simply 'bad air' in any context — is dead. The word now means only the disease, and the miasma theory it was named after is discredited.

curfew.currentMeaning: A regulation requiring people to remain indoors during specified hours

chain.note: The root verb: to cover something
Medieval towns required all fires to be covered at a certain hour to prevent urban conflagrations. The 'cuevrefeu' bell rang to signal: cover your fire.

chain.meaning: the evening bell ordering fires to be covered
chain.note: The Norman French form entered English law. The curfew was literally a fire safety regulation.

chain.meaning: a regulation requiring people to remain indoors
chain.note: The fire is gone from the word. But 'curfew' literally means 'cover the fire' — a medieval fire safety bell that became a general order to stay inside.

deadBranches.meaning: the bell that signals the covering of fires
deadBranches.note: The literal meaning — the actual bell rung at evening to remind people to cover their hearths — is dead. Modern curfews have nothing to do with fire.

chain.meaning: to set, to put, to do
chain.note: A fundamental root meaning placement and action
'De-' (from) + 'habere' (to have). To owe is to 'have from' — something you have that comes from someone else, and must be returned.

chain.meaning: that which is owed, a debt
chain.note: The past participle became the noun. A debit is a debt.
Borrowed from French, without the 'b'

Scholars added the 'b' to show the word's descent from Latin 'debitum'. The 'b' is silent — a fossil of Renaissance pedantry. You can see the Latin debt inside the English word, but you can't hear it.

cognates.meaning: debt, guilt (same concept — what you owe)

deadBranches.note: The natural English form 'dette' was replaced by the learned 'debt' — a Renaissance spelling reform that inserted a silent letter to assert classical credentials. The spoken word never changed; only the spelling was fossilized.

dexterity.currentMeaning: Skill in performing tasks, especially with the hands

chain.note: Right-handedness was the norm. The right hand was the skillful hand.
'Dexter' meant both 'right side' and 'skillful'. The right hand was the good hand — the left was 'sinister'.
The abstract noun: the quality of being right-handed, hence skillful
The directional meaning ('right side') was lost; only 'skill' remained

The right hand is still inside the word. Dexterity literally means 'right-handedness' — the left-handed were excluded from the concept of skill. Language encoded right-handed bias into the word for competence.

deadBranches.note: The paired opposite: 'sinister' (left) developed meanings of evil and bad luck, while 'dexter' (right) meant skill and favorability. The left-handed dead branch became the English word 'sinister' — a parallel etymological fate.

astronaut.currentMeaning: A person trained to travel in a spacecraft

chain.note: The ancient root for star — the same root in 'disaster' (bad star) and 'asterisk' (little star)
The Greek form of the star-root
The root that gives us 'nautical' and 'nausea' (seasickness). A sailor is a 'nautes'.

chain.meaning: a person who travels in space
chain.note: Coined by science fiction writers: 'astron' (star) + 'nautes' (sailor). An astronaut is a star-sailor. The word was coined before anyone had ever been to space.

deadBranches.note: The original Greek 'nautes' meant a literal sailor on a literal ship. That concrete meaning is dead in 'astronaut' — the ship is metaphorical now, the sea replaced by vacuum.

odd.currentMeaning: Different from what is usual; strange

chain.note: Originally: a point, a triangle, a pointed piece of land jutting into the sea. Something with three points or three corners.
Oddi came to mean 'third point' — the point that doesn't have a pair. An odd number is the one left over.
Borrowed from Norse. An odd shoe was one without a pair. An odd man was one without a partner.
The meaning drifted from 'unmatched' to 'unusual' to 'strange'. Being the odd one out was being strange.

chain.meaning: strange, peculiar, different from the usual
chain.note: A triangle in Old Norse became strangeness in English. The geometry became psychology. The odd one out — the one without a pair — is still the root meaning.

deadBranches.note: The original geometric meaning — a point or triangle — is completely dead. The geographic sense survives in Scandinavian place names (Reykjavik's Oddi), but the geometry is gone.

villain.currentMeaning: A person guilty of a crime or wicked act

chain.note: A villa was a farm. The people who worked it were the lowest social class.
A 'villanus' was a person bound to the villa — a serf, a peasant, a rural worker.
In feudal society, 'vilain' meant a person of low birth — a peasant. The aristocracy used it as a class slur.
The class meaning started shifting toward moral meaning. If peasants were bad, then 'villain' meant 'bad person'. Class prejudice became a word for evil.

chain.meaning: a person guilty of wicked or criminal acts
chain.note: The farm is gone. The peasant is gone. What remains is pure evil. 'Villain' is a 2000-year journey from 'farm worker' to 'evil mastermind'. Class hatred froze into language.

cognates.meaning: ugly, nasty (the class meaning is archaic)

deadBranches.meaning: a peasant, a serf (class designation, not moral judgment)
deadBranches.note: The original meaning — a social class, not a moral category — is dead. Villains used to be farmers. The word became a weapon, then lost its original target.

silly.currentMeaning: Having or showing a lack of common sense; frivolous

chain.note: To be 'gesælig' was to be blessed by God — happy, prosperous, lucky. A deeply positive word.
The prefix 'ge-' dropped. The word still meant 'blessed'.
The meaning started to rot. 'Blessed' became 'innocent' became 'pitiable'. The blessed were naive; the naive were weak; the weak were contemptible.
The descent: blessed → innocent → pitiable → weak → foolish.
The greatest semantic tragedy in English. 'Silly' started as 'blessed' and ended as 'foolish'. The word's journey is a linguistic fall from grace — from heaven to absurdity in 900 years.

deadBranches.note: The original theological meaning — touched by divine blessing — is completely extinct. German 'selig' preserves it, but English 'silly' has fallen entirely into the secular and contemptuous.

fascinate.currentMeaning: To attract and hold attentively by unique qualities

chain.meaning: witchcraft, spell, evil eye, phallic amulet
chain.note: A 'fascinum' was a phallic charm worn to ward off the evil eye. The word meant both the amulet and the magic it countered — or cast.

chain.meaning: to cast a spell on, to bewitch
chain.note: To fascinate was to put someone under a spell — to bind them with magic, to enchant them against their will.
The magical meaning was still literal: to cast a spell
The magic weakened to metaphor. To fascinate is to hold someone spellbound — but the spell is figurative now. The witchcraft is still in the word, buried under centuries of metaphor.

deadBranches.note: The original physical object — the actual amulet — is dead. The fascinum was a real thing Romans wore. Now it's just a ghost inside the word 'fascinate', invisible to most speakers.

chain.meaning: the city of Nîmes in southern France
chain.note: Nîmes was a major textile center. Weavers there produced a distinctive sturdy cloth.
The full name: 'serge de Nîmes' — the serge fabric from the city of Nîmes
English buyers shortened the French phrase to 'serge de Nim', then just 'de Nim'

'De Nîmes' → 'denim'. The fabric is named after a French city. Every pair of jeans carries the name of Nîmes, compressed into five letters. Jeans are from Genoa; denim is from Nîmes. Your pants are a map of the Mediterranean.

deadBranches.note: The word 'serge' (the type of weave) was dropped entirely. No one says 'serge denim'. The 'serge' is a dead branch — the weave specification died, but the place name survived.

decide.currentMeaning: To come to a resolution; to choose

chain.note: The root: cutting, striking, violence
The Latin verb: to cut, to hew, to strike down

chain.meaning: to cut off, to resolve, to decide
chain.note: 'De-' (off) + 'caedere' (to cut). To decide was to cut off alternatives. Decision is surgical: you cut away the options you don't want.
The cutting was becoming metaphorical

chain.meaning: to come to a resolution, to choose
chain.note: Every decision is a cutting. To decide is to cut off — to sever the alternatives you didn't choose. The knife is still in the word. Decide shares a root with 'homicide', 'fratricide', 'suicide'. All of them end with the same cutting.

deadBranches.meaning: to cut off, to fall down (physical sense)
deadBranches.note: The original physical meaning — literally cutting something off, or falling down — is dead. Only the mental metaphor survives: the surgical act became a cognitive one.

digit.currentMeaning: A number; a finger or toe

chain.note: The root: pointing, showing. A finger points. A number points to a quantity.
The Latin word for finger. People counted on their fingers. Fingers were the original numbers.
The word split: it meant both 'finger' and 'number from 0 to 9' — because the ten numerals correspond to the ten fingers

chain.meaning: a number (0-9); a finger or toe
chain.note: The connection between fingers and numbers is still visible. Every digital device is, etymologically, a finger device. The 'digital age' is the age of counting on your fingers.

deadBranches.meaning: the width of a finger (as a unit of measurement)
deadBranches.note: Roman 'digitus' was also a unit of length — the width of a finger, about 3/4 of an inch. This measurement sense is dead. The finger-unit became abstract numbers.

testify.currentMeaning: To give evidence as a witness

chain.note: The number three — the basis of 'testis'
A 'testis' was a witness. The word may derive from 'tri-stis' (third person standing by) — a witness was the third party present at a transaction between two others.

chain.meaning: to bear witness, to make a will
chain.note: To testify was to witness. A 'testament' was a witnessed statement — a will.

chain.meaning: to give evidence as a witness in court
chain.note: The witness is still in the word. To testify is to stand as a third party and say what you saw. The 'three' is still there — the third person watching two others make an agreement.

deadBranches.meaning: witness (the literal person, not the abstract act)
deadBranches.note: The Latin noun 'testis' — meaning both 'witness' and, anatomically, 'testicle' — is the source of much debate. The anatomical meaning may be unrelated (from a different root), but the confusion between witnessing and the anatomical term is ancient.

chain.meaning: a divine power, a lesser deity, a guiding spirit
chain.note: A 'daimon' was not evil. It was a divine being — a spirit between gods and humans. Socrates said his 'daimonion' was a divine inner voice that guided him.

chain.meaning: a spirit, one's lot or fortune
chain.note: A daimon could be good or bad. It was your spiritual guide — your genius, your tutelary spirit.
Christian writers redefined pagan spirits as evil. The old gods became demons. 'Daimon' shifted from 'divine guide' to 'evil spirit'.
Borrowed from Greek with the Christian negative meaning

The original Greek 'daimon' was a benevolent guide. Christian theology converted it into a force of evil. The word's journey is a story of religious conquest — one culture's angels became another culture's demons.

deadBranches.meaning: a benevolent personal spirit, a divine guide
deadBranches.note: The original Socratic meaning — a personal divine spirit, a inner guide — is dead. No one uses 'demon' to mean 'guardian angel' anymore. The Christians won the semantic war.

chain.note: Wyrd was fate itself — the force that governed all events, even the gods. It was not 'weird' in the modern sense; it was the most serious concept in the Anglo-Saxon universe.
The word still meant fate. The 'Weird Sisters' in Macbeth were the Fates — the three goddesses who controlled destiny.
After Macbeth, 'weird' became associated with the supernatural and uncanny. The witches were 'weird' — and the word absorbed their strangeness.

Fate became strangeness. The most profound concept in Anglo-Saxon metaphysics — wyrd, the force that governs all events — became a word for 'kind of odd'. Shakespeare's witches completed the journey from destiny to oddity.

cognates.meaning: fate, destiny (one of the three Norns)

deadBranches.meaning: fate as a cosmic force (theological/philosophical sense)
deadBranches.note: The philosophical concept of wyrd — the Anglo-Saxon understanding of fate as an impersonal cosmic force — is dead. 'Weird' now means 'slightly strange'. The philosophy was lost; only the strangeness remained.

notorious.currentMeaning: Famous or well-known, typically for some bad quality or deed

chain.note: The past participle of 'noscere' (to know). 'Notus' meant simply: known.
Notorious meant 'well-known'. Period. No negative connotation. A notorious fact was simply a widely known fact.
Borrowed from Latin as a legal term — a notorious fact was one that needed no proof because everyone knew it

The meaning soured. Being 'well-known' became associated with being well-known for bad things. The word now implies infamy — but the original Latin meant nothing more than 'famous'. Notorious = known. The negativity is a modern addition.

deadBranches.note: The original legal sense — a fact so well-known it requires no proof — is dead in common usage. The word has shifted entirely from a neutral descriptive term to a negative judgment.

hypocrite.currentMeaning: A person who claims to have virtues they don't possess

chain.note: 'Hypo' (under) + 'krinein' (to judge, decide). An actor was someone who performed under judgment — who answered from behind a mask.
The meaning jumped from the theater to morality. An actor pretends; a hypocrite pretends. The metaphorical leap was natural.
Borrowed from Greek as a moral and religious term

chain.meaning: a person who pretends to virtues they lack
chain.note: The theatrical meaning was completely lost. The moral meaning dominated.

chain.meaning: a person who claims virtues they don't possess
chain.note: Every hypocrite is, etymologically, an actor. The word comes from the Greek stage. A hypocrite is someone still performing — wearing a mask of virtue, playing a role. The theater is still in the moral judgment.

deadBranches.note: The original theatrical sense — literally an actor on stage — is dead in the English word. Greek still uses a related word for 'actor', but English 'hypocrite' has no theatrical meaning at all. The stage became a moral category.

bankrupt.currentMeaning: A person or entity unable to pay debts

chain.note: Italian moneychangers conducted business at tables ('banche') in the marketplace. The table was the bank.
When a moneychanger went out of business, his table was physically broken — 'banca rotta'. The broken table was public proof of financial ruin.
The Italian phrase was borrowed into French as a single word

A bankrupt is a broken table. When medieval Italian moneychangers failed, their tables were smashed. The physical destruction became the metaphor for financial ruin. Every bankruptcy begins with a broken bench.

deadBranches.note: The original physical act — literally breaking a moneychanger's table to publicly signal their failure — is dead. The practice died with medieval markets, but the word survived as pure metaphor.

gymnasium.currentMeaning: A room or building for physical exercise

chain.note: The root: naked. The Greeks exercised naked.

chain.meaning: a place for physical and intellectual education
chain.note: A gymnasium was where Greek men trained naked — both physically and intellectually. It was a school as much as an exercise ground. Plato taught in a gymnasium.
Borrowed from Greek, but the Romans wore clothes to exercise

Every gym is named after nakedness. 'Gym' comes from 'gymnos' — naked. The Greeks exercised nude, and they named their training grounds accordingly. The word has kept its name for 2500 years. The clothes are the only thing that changed.

deadBranches.meaning: a combined physical and intellectual school
deadBranches.note: The original Greek gymnasium was both body and mind — philosophy, mathematics, and wrestling under one roof. The intellectual component is dead in the English word. A modern gym is all body, no mind.

plagiarize.currentMeaning: To take someone else's work and pass it off as one's own

chain.meaning: net, snare, trap for catching animals
chain.note: A plaga was a hunter's net — a device for catching living things

chain.meaning: kidnapper, stealer of slaves or children
chain.note: A 'plagiarius' was someone who caught people in a net — a kidnapper, a human trafficker. The poet Martial used 'plagiarius' metaphorically to accuse someone of stealing his verses.
The kidnapping metaphor stuck. Literary theft was conceptualized as a form of kidnapping — stealing someone's brain-child.

chain.meaning: to steal and pass off another's work as one's own
chain.note: Plagiarism is kidnapping. The word comes from Latin for 'snatching someone in a net'. To plagiarize is to kidnap words — to steal someone's intellectual child. The violence of the original metaphor is still in the word.

deadBranches.note: The original meaning — a literal kidnapper who snatched people in nets — is dead. The physical crime became a metaphorical one. But Italian 'plagio' still means both plagiarism and brainwashing — the sense of capturing minds survives.

mortgage.currentMeaning: A legal agreement for borrowing money to buy property

chain.note: Death. The beginning of the word.
A pledge — something given as security for a debt
'Mort' (dead) + 'gage' (pledge). A mortgage was a 'dead pledge' — a pledge that dies when the debt is paid, or a pledge that kills you if you can't pay. Either way, death is the concept.

chain.meaning: a dead pledge, a property security
chain.note: The French legal term entered English property law

chain.meaning: a loan for buying property, secured on the property
chain.note: Your mortgage is a death pledge. The word literally means 'dead pledge'. Every homeowner carries a death pledge. The etymology is terrifyingly honest.

deadBranches.note: The opposite of a 'mortgage' (dead pledge) was a 'vifgage' (living pledge) — where the income from the pledged land paid off the debt. The 'living pledge' concept is dead. Only the 'dead pledge' survived.

sermon.currentMeaning: A talk on a religious or moral subject, given during a church service

chain.note: 'Sermo' was simply speech — any connected discourse. It was neutral, even pleasant. A sermo was a chat, a discussion, a talk.
Christian writers specialized the word: a 'sermo' was now specifically a religious discourse, a homily. The general 'talk' meaning narrowed to 'pious talk'.
Borrowed from ecclesiastical Latin with the religious meaning fixed

chain.meaning: a talk on a religious or moral subject
chain.note: A sermon used to be just a conversation. The Latin 'sermo' meant any talk. Then the Church took it, and now a sermon is something you sit through. The word's journey from 'chat' to 'lecture' is a miniature history of institutional power over language.

deadBranches.note: The original meaning — simply 'conversation, talk' — is dead. A 'sermo' between friends was just a chat. Now 'sermon' means only a moralizing monologue. The conversation became a lecture.

prestige.currentMeaning: Widespread respect and admiration attracted by achievements

chain.meaning: to bind fast, to dazzle, to blind
chain.note: 'Prae-' (before) + 'stringere' (to bind). To dazzle or blind — to trick the eyes.
Praestigiae were conjuring tricks — the deceptions of a stage magician. A 'praestigiator' was a juggler, a trickster.
In French, 'prestige' still meant deception — a trick played on the eyes
English borrowed the word with its original meaning: a trick, a deception, a false appearance

The word flipped. From 'deception' to 'respect'. How? The dazzling quality of a conjuring trick became the dazzling quality of reputation. Prestige is still a kind of illusion — the glamour that makes people admire you. The trick is still in the word.

deadBranches.meaning: a juggler, a conjuror, a trickster
deadBranches.note: The original meaning — a stage magician, a literal trickster — is dead. The word has been sanitized. Prestige used to mean 'deception'. Now it means 'admiration'. The trickster became a compliment.

feisty.currentMeaning: Aggressive, excitable, full of nervous energy

chain.note: The root: a fart. 'Fist' was a vulgar word for flatulence.

chain.meaning: a stinking dog, a worthless mongrel
chain.note: A 'fysting cur' was a farting dog — a small, aggressive, stinking mongrel. The phrase described the worst kind of dog.

chain.meaning: a small, aggressive dog; a worthless person
chain.note: The word narrowed: a feist was specifically a small, snappy, aggressive dog

In American dialect, 'feisty' became an adjective for small, aggressive dogs — then for small, aggressive people. The fart is gone. The dog is gone. What remains is the spirit. A feisty person is etymologically a farting dog.

deadBranches.note: The original literal meaning — a fart — is completely dead. 'Fist' now means only a clenched hand (from a different root). The flatulence sense is buried so deep that most dictionaries mark it as etymologically uncertain.
